route.title: Set Up Your First Board
route.summary: Learn where each piece goes at the start of a chess game. The board has 64 squares and each piece has its own home spot.

challenge.prompt: Set up a real chess board or draw one on paper with all 16 pieces on each side in their starting positions. Take a photo showing the whole board.

route.title: Move Like a Pawn
route.summary: Pawns move forward one square at a time, but on their first move they can jump two squares. They capture diagonally, not straight ahead.

challenge.prompt: Start with pawns on their home squares. Write down three legal pawn moves you could make (like 'pawn from e2 to e4'). Then explain why a pawn CANNOT move backwards.

route.title: Command Your Rooks and Bishops
route.summary: Rooks slide up-down or left-right any number of squares. Bishops slide diagonally any number of squares. They can't jump over pieces.

challenge.prompt: On a board, place one rook and one bishop. Use coins or paper to mark ALL the squares each piece can move to. Take a photo and circle which squares the bishop can reach that the rook cannot.

route.title: Master the Knight's L-Jump
route.summary: Knights move in an L-shape: two squares in one direction, then one square perpendicular. They're the only piece that can jump over others.

challenge.prompt: Place a knight on the center of the board (d4 or e4). List all eight squares it can jump to. Then explain in your own words why a knight on a white square always lands on a black square next.

route.title: Protect Your King and Use Your Queen
route.summary: The king moves one square in any direction. The queen moves any number of squares in any direction (like a rook and bishop combined). Your king can never move into danger.

challenge.prompt: Set up a position with your king, your queen, and three enemy pawns. Show a photo where your queen is protecting your king from an attack. Draw arrows showing how your queen blocks the danger.

route.title: Deliver Checkmate in One Move
route.summary: Checkmate means the enemy king is attacked and has no escape. The game ends immediately. You need to trap the king so it can't move to safety.

challenge.prompt: Create three different board positions where you can checkmate the enemy king in just one move. Take photos of all three setups and circle which piece delivers checkmate in each.

route.title: Castle Your King to Safety
route.summary: Castling is a special move where your king slides two squares toward a rook, and the rook hops over to the other side. You can only do it if neither piece has moved yet and there's nothing between them.

challenge.prompt: Explain the three rules that must be true before you can castle. Then describe a situation where castling would be a smart move to protect your king from danger.

route.title: Win Material Through Captures
route.summary: Each piece has a value: pawn=1, knight=3, bishop=3, rook=5, queen=9. Trading a knight for a rook is good because you gain 2 points of material.

challenge.prompt: Play or set up a position where you can capture an enemy rook by sacrificing only a pawn or bishop. Explain why this trade helps you win, using the point values.

route.title: Control the Center Four Squares
route.summary: The four center squares (d4, e4, d5, e5) are the most important territory. Pieces in the center can reach more of the board and control the game.

challenge.prompt: Play the first 4 moves of a game (you and a friend or computer) where you fight for control of the center. Take a photo and write down which pieces you used and why controlling the center gives you an advantage.

route.title: Solve a Two-Move Checkmate Puzzle
route.summary: Advanced checkmates require setting up a trap first. You make one move to force the enemy into a bad spot, then checkmate on your second move.

challenge.prompt: Find a two-move checkmate puzzle online or in a book. Write down the position (where each piece is), then explain both moves: what you do first and why it forces checkmate on move two.

route.title: Play Your First Full Game
route.summary: Put everything together: opening moves to control the center, protect your king, develop your pieces, and hunt for checkmate or win material.

challenge.prompt: Play a complete game against a friend, family member, or computer (easy mode). Take a photo of the final position. Write 3-5 sentences about what you did well and one mistake you made.

route.title: Analyze and Improve Your Strategy
route.summary: Good chess players review their games to find better moves. Look for moments where you could have won material, avoided danger, or checkmated faster.

challenge.prompt: Replay your game from waypoint 11 or play a new one. Pick three moments where you made a choice. For each, explain what you did and what you could have done better. Show you understand why one move is stronger than another.
